name: INA226AIDGSR
title: 36 V, 16-bit current, voltage and power monitor with I2C/SMBus interface and alert output
summary: The INA226 measures the drop across an external shunt resistor (IN+ to IN–) and the voltage on a separate bus pin (VBUS) with a 16-bit delta-sigma ADC, then multiplies them internally so current in amperes and power in watts can be read straight from registers over an I2C or SMBus interface. The shunt and bus inputs work at common-mode voltages from 0 V to 36 V whatever the chip's own 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply, so it can sit on the high side or the low side of a load. Conversion time and averaging are programmable, an open-drain Alert pin signals one chosen limit or conversion-ready, and two address pins give 16 bus addresses. It comes in a 10-pin VSSOP (DGS) for –40°C to 125°C.
key_figures: I2C / SMBus, up to 2.94 MHz, 16 addresses

notes: All part numbers are the 10-pin VSSOP; they differ in reel size (2500 or 250), lead finish and moisture sensitivity level.
An automotive-qualified version, INA226-Q1, exists.

circuits.title: High-side sensing, 12 V supply, 10 A load
circuits.description: A 2 mΩ shunt sits between a 12 V supply and a 10 A load. IN+ takes the supply end, IN– the load end, and VBUS also ties to the load end, where the bus reads 11.98 V at 10 A. VS is bypassed by 0.1 µF; SDA, SCL and Alert are each pulled up to VS. A0 and A1 are grounded, which sets address 1000000. With a 1 mA/bit Current_LSB the Calibration value for this circuit is 2560.

circuits.title: High-side sensing with input filter
circuits.description: The shunt sits between a 0 V to 36 V supply and the load. Each sense line passes through a series resistor of 10 Ω or less, and a 0.1 µF to 1 µF ceramic capacitor across IN+ and IN– after them forms a differential low-pass filter against transients at the ADC's sampling harmonics. VBUS reads the supply side of the shunt. VS has a 0.1 µF bypass; SDA, SCL and Alert are pulled up to VS; A0 and A1 leave the circuit as terminals.

circuits.title: High-side sensing
circuits.description: The shunt is placed between the bus supply (0 V to 36 V) and the load, IN+ on the supply end and IN– on the load end. VBUS connects to the bus supply. The chip runs from its own 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply with a 0.1 µF bypass; SDA, SCL and Alert are pulled up to VS.

circuits.title: Low-side sensing
circuits.description: The shunt is placed between the load and ground, IN+ on the load end and IN– on the ground end. VBUS still connects to the bus supply, so bus voltage and power are measured while the current is sensed at ground level. The chip runs from its own 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply with a 0.1 µF bypass; SDA, SCL and Alert are pulled up to VS.

operation.text: The ADC converts two quantities: the differential voltage between IN+ and IN– (shunt voltage, taken relative to IN–) and the VBUS pin voltage referred to GND. From the shunt result and the Calibration Register the chip computes current, and from current and the bus result it computes power. These sums run in the background and add nothing to conversion time.
Common-mode range and supply are independent, so there is no power-up order: the bus may be live with VS off and the reverse. The inputs withstand 0 V to 36 V with or without VS applied.

With MODE = 111 (the reset state) the ADC alternates a shunt conversion and a bus conversion without stopping. Each pair's results and the derived current and power are accumulated until the set number of averages is reached; then all four output registers update together and hold until the next complete set. Reading the outputs does not disturb a conversion. Modes 101 and 110 convert only shunt or only bus.
Writing MODE 001, 010 or 011 starts one single-shot set of conversions. Another shot needs another write to the Configuration Register, even with the same mode value.
MODE 000 or 100 cuts quiescent current and stops current into the inputs. Registers stay readable and writable. Writing an active mode wakes the chip; full recovery takes 40 µs.

CVRF (Mask/Enable bit 3) sets once all conversions, averaging and multiplications of a set are complete. It clears on any write to the Configuration Register other than one selecting power-down, or on a read of the Mask/Enable Register.
With the Calibration Register at zero, the Current and Power registers stay at zero. Shunt and bus voltages are still converted from power-up with no programming at all.

The open-drain Alert pin follows one of five limit functions selected in the Mask/Enable Register: shunt over-limit (SOL), shunt under-limit (SUL), bus over-limit (BOL), bus under-limit (BUL) or power over-limit (POL), compared with the single Alert Limit Register. Only one function is active; if several are set, the highest bit wins. Shunt limits are checked after every shunt conversion; bus and power limits after every bus conversion. Conversion-ready can drive the pin as well; when both are enabled, AFF and CVRF in the Mask/Enable Register tell which caused the alert. Polarity is set by APOL. In latch mode the pin and AFF stay asserted until the Mask/Enable Register is read (or the Configuration Register written); in transparent mode they clear after the next conversion with no fault. An unused Alert pin may float.

Shunt and bus conversion times are set separately from 140 µs to 8.244 ms, and 1 to 1024 results are averaged. Longer conversions and more averages cut noise; the best accuracy comes from the longest times and most averages the system's update rate allows. Example: 588 µs on both channels with 4 averages updates about every 4.7 ms; so does 4.156 ms shunt, 588 µs bus with 1 average.

The ADC is a delta-sigma type sampling at a typical 500 kHz (±30%). Only transients at its harmonics, 1 MHz and above, call for an input filter: a series resistor of 10 Ω or less in each input with a ceramic capacitor of 0.1 µF to 1 µF across IN+ and IN–.

The inputs tolerate 40 V differential. A load-side short can put the full supply across the shunt, and clearing it can kick back inductively past the 40 V differential and common-mode ratings; a transient-voltage suppressor with enough bulk capacitance controls this. Without large electrolytics beside the shunt, a fast dV/dt from a hard short can trigger the input ESD structures; 10 Ω in series with each input was shown in test to protect up to 40 V, with little effect on accuracy.

Current and power are scaled by the Calibration Register. Choosing it for the smallest Current_LSB gives the most resolution; choosing a round Current_LSB gives direct readings. Example: 15 A maximum gives 457.7 µA/bit minimum; with 1 mA/bit and 2 mΩ the Calibration value is 2560 (A00h), and the power LSB is 25 mW/bit. The value can also be trimmed against an external ammeter to cancel system error.

Registers are volatile: any non-default setting has to be written again after every power-up. Setting RST (Configuration bit 15) resets all registers like a power-on reset and clears itself. Writing the Configuration Register halts a conversion in progress and starts a new one with the new settings.

The INA226 is a target only, on I2C or SMBus. SDA and SCL are open drain with spike suppression and Schmitt triggers. Fast mode runs 1 kHz to 400 kHz and high-speed mode 1 kHz to 2.94 MHz. Bytes go most significant first. A write sends the address byte, a register pointer byte and two data bytes; a read returns two bytes from the register the pointer last named, and the pointer stays put for repeated reads. A 28 ms SCL-low timeout resets the interface so it cannot lock the bus.

After a start, the controller sends the HS controller code 00001XXX at 400 kHz or less. The INA226 does not acknowledge it but switches its input filters for 2.94 MHz; after a repeated start, transfers run at up to 2.94 MHz. HS operation lasts across repeated starts; a stop condition ends it and restores fast/standard filtering.

The chip answers the SMBus Alert Response address 0001 100 read: a device holding an alert acknowledges and sends its own address. If several respond, arbitration decides, and a loser keeps Alert low until its interrupt is cleared.
VS may be well below the monitored bus, for example 5 V while the bus is at 36 V. A bypass capacitor, typically 0.1 µF, sits right at VS and GND; noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more.

Take IN+ and IN– from the shunt by Kelvin (4-wire) connections so only the shunt's own resistance lies between them; any extra copper carrying the load current in that path adds large errors with a milliohm shunt. Keep the VS bypass capacitor tight against the VS and GND pins. VBUS connects to the power-supply rail.
